clinicalPearls: Urethral prolapse is circumferential eversion of the distal urethral mucosa through the external meatus, forming a doughnut-shaped ring of tissue around the urethral opening
It has a characteristic bimodal distribution, occurring in prepubertal girls and in postmenopausal women, both low-oestrogen states
Typical presentations are painless vaginal or vulval bleeding or spotting, a visible periurethral mass, and sometimes dysuria or voiding difficulty
In young girls it is an important and benign cause of genital bleeding that can be mistaken for trauma or abuse, so recognition prevents misdirected concern
The key clinical feature is that the prolapsed mucosa surrounds the meatus symmetrically, distinguishing it from an eccentric caruncle or other periurethral lesion
It must be differentiated from a urethral caruncle, prolapsing ureterocele, periurethral cyst, and, importantly, urethral or other malignancy in older women
Uncomplicated cases are often managed conservatively with topical oestrogen, sitz baths, and treatment of any constipation or straining
Surgical excision of the prolapsed mucosa is reserved for strangulated, thrombosed, necrotic, or non-resolving cases, or when the diagnosis is uncertain and tissue is needed
A strangulated, thrombosed, or necrotic prolapse causing pain or urinary retention warrants prompt urological assessment
reference.pathophysiology: Urethral prolapse results from eversion of the distal urethral mucosa through the meatus. A relative deficiency of oestrogen, as in prepubertal girls and postmenopausal women, weakens the periurethral supporting tissues and the attachments between the inner longitudinal and outer circular smooth muscle layers of the urethra. Poor cohesion between these layers, combined with raised intra-abdominal pressure from straining, coughing, or constipation, allows the redundant mucosa to protrude and evert around the meatus. The exposed mucosa becomes congested, oedematous, and friable, and if venous drainage is compromised it may thrombose, strangulate, or necrose.
additionalDifferentials: Periurethral cyst or abscess (e.g. Skene gland)
Genital trauma (a key consideration in children)
additionalInvestigations: Careful clinical examination confirming circumferential eversion around the meatus
Confirmation that the mass surrounds the urethral opening, often by passing or visualising a catheter through the central lumen
Urinalysis and culture if infection or dysuria is present
Biopsy or excision histology where malignancy is suspected, particularly in older women
Examination under anaesthesia in children if the diagnosis is unclear or examination is difficult
redFlags: Strangulated, thrombosed, or necrotic prolapsed mucosa
Acute urinary retention from the prolapse
Suspicion of malignancy in a postmenopausal woman with an atypical or firm periurethral lesion
Uncertain diagnosis where abuse or trauma is being wrongly considered in a child, or genuine trauma is missed
reference.prognosis: Urethral prolapse is benign and generally responds well to conservative measures, particularly topical oestrogen, with a good prognosis and low recurrence when precipitating factors such as straining are addressed. Surgical excision is curative for complicated or refractory cases. Prompt recognition in children avoids unnecessary distress and investigation, while vigilance in older women ensures malignancy is not overlooked.
pitfalls: Mistaking benign prolapse in a child for signs of trauma or abuse, or vice versa
Confusing it with a urethral caruncle or, in older women, with malignancy
Overlooking a strangulated or necrotic prolapse needing surgical intervention
Failing to address straining and constipation, allowing recurrence
Not obtaining histology when the lesion is atypical in a postmenopausal woman
management: Offer first-line topical oestrogen cream to restore the atrophic periurethral tissues in prepubertal girls and postmenopausal women
Advise conservative measures including sitz baths, good hygiene and treatment of the local inflammation
Address precipitating raised intra-abdominal pressure by treating constipation, chronic cough and straining
Attempt gentle manual reduction, and manage a strangulated, thrombosed or necrotic prolapse as an acute problem
Reserve surgical excision of the redundant prolapsed mucosa for refractory, strangulated or necrotic tissue
Reassure that the condition is benign, and in young girls recognise it explicitly to avoid misattributing genital bleeding to trauma or abuse
